scope: Ranks 251–1500, resolved current similar-word teaching and typed recall. Includes retained baseline cards; do not infer no synonyms from unchanged status.
grading: Only exact headword/explicit alternatives pass after case/edge-punctuation normalization. Accent/spelling slips and recognized inflections get score-free correction opportunities, not immediate rejection. Dictionary-form recall is explicit. Cloze and recognition acceptance are separate. Broad main teaching examples may show a different legitimate sense from selected typed cue; classify teaching alignment separately from false facts.

sections.title: To add
sections.text: Agregar and añadir overlap for adding an item. Incluir, incorporar and sumar also fit adding a name to a list. Sumar is not restricted to arithmetic; its broader uses include adding people or things to a whole.
examples: Añade otro nombre a la lista.
Add another name to the list.

sections.title: To understand
sections.text: Comprender and entender overlap for understanding. Comprender can also mean include or comprise; that sense is separate from understanding.

sections.title: To need
sections.text: Necesitar and requerir overlap in the sense of needing. Requerir can also mean formally request or demand; these additional uses are not interchangeable in every sentence.

sections.title: To increase
sections.text: Aumentar and incrementar both describe an increase in an amount. Crecer usually presents the subject itself as growing, rather than directly increasing an object.

sections.title: To reduce
sections.text: Reducir and disminuir overlap when making an amount smaller. Disminuir can also be intransitive: la presión disminuye.

sections.title: To cause
sections.text: Causar, provocar and ocasionar can describe causing a problem. Provocar also means provoke a person; that additional meaning is not automatic for the other verbs.

sections.title: To choose
sections.text: Elegir, escoger and seleccionar overlap for choosing an option. Elegir also describes electing someone to office.

sections.title: To send
sections.text: Enviar and mandar overlap for sending a letter. Mandar also means command; enviar does not carry that sense.

sections.title: To return
sections.text: Regresar, volver and retornar overlap for returning to a place. Volver a + infinitive means do something again; regresar does not substitute for that repeated-action construction.

sections.title: To walk
sections.text: Caminar and andar overlap for walking. Andar also describes how something works or how someone is doing.

sections.title: To place
sections.text: Colocar, poner, situar and ubicar overlap for placing something. Their broader uses differ: poner has many change-of-state constructions, and situar/ubicar emphasize location.
examples: Coloca la mesa junto a la ventana.
Place the table next to the window.

sections.title: To stop
sections.text: Detener and parar overlap when stopping a vehicle. Detener also means detain someone; detenerse is the usual reflexive form when the subject stops.

sections.title: To throw
sections.text: Echar, lanzar and tirar can describe throwing a ball. Tirar also means throw away, and tirar de means pull on; echar has many fixed expressions.

sections.title: To express
sections.text: Expresar and manifestar overlap for expressing an opinion. Manifestar can also make a condition evident; manifestarse can mean demonstrate in public.

sections.title: To suggest
sections.text: Proponer and sugerir overlap for putting forward an idea. Sugerir can also mean imply or evoke something without explicitly proposing it.

sections.title: To want
sections.text: Desear and querer overlap for wishing for something. Querer also expresses affection; that meaning needs a person or other appropriate object.

sections.title: To buy
sections.text: Comprar means buy. Adquirir can mean acquire by purchase but also by other means, so acquire alone does not entail payment.

sections.title: To constitute
sections.text: Formar, constituir and conformar overlap when parts make up a whole. Conformarse con means settle for; it is a different construction.
examples: Three people make up the team.

sections.title: To analyze
sections.text: Analizar emphasizes examining parts or relationships. Examinar and estudiar also fit examining something in detail; examinar can additionally describe a simpler inspection.

sections.title: To protect
sections.text: Proteger and defender overlap for protection. Defender emphasizes defending against a threat and also applies to arguing for a position.

sections.title: To move
sections.text: Trasladar specifies transfer to another place. Mover also covers motion without a change of location, such as moving an arm.
examples: Trasladan los muebles a otra casa.
They move the furniture to another house.

sections.title: To abandon
sections.text: Abandonar emphasizes leaving behind or giving up. Dejar also means leave, let or lend; those broader uses are not all abandonment.

sections.title: End
sections.text: Fin and final overlap for an ending. Término can also mean end, while conclusión may be a conclusion reached by reasoning; those broader senses need context.
examples: El final de la película es triste.
The end of the film is sad.

sections.title: Result
sections.text: Resultado, consecuencia and efecto overlap for outcomes of actions. Resultado also names a score, and efecto has scientific and legal uses that need their own context.
examples: Fue una consecuencia de la decisión.
It was a consequence of the decision.

sections.title: Reason
sections.text: Motivo and razón overlap for a reason to act. Causa names what produces an effect, which need not be someone's conscious motive.
examples: Explica el motivo de su decisión.
She explains the reason for her decision.

sections.title: Place
sections.text: Sitio and lugar overlap for a place. Sitio also appears in sitio web, while lugar has expressions such as tener lugar, meaning take place.

sections.title: School
sections.text: Escuela and colegio overlap for schools, with differences in local education systems. Colegio can also be a professional association; universidad is a different educational level.

sections.title: Teacher
sections.text: Profesor and maestro overlap for a teacher. Maestro also means master or expert, and the preferred term for a schoolteacher varies by place and level.

sections.title: Student
sections.text: Estudiante and alumno overlap for a school student. Alumno emphasizes the relationship to a teacher or institution; estudiante emphasizes studying.

sections.title: Doctor
sections.text: Médico and doctor overlap for a physician. Doctor also refers to a person with a doctorate, who need not be a physician.
examples: La médica trabaja en el hospital.
The doctor works at the hospital.

sections.title: Company
sections.text: Compañía and empresa overlap for a company. Negocio is a business or commercial activity and can also mean a deal; compañía also means companionship.
examples: She works at a small company.

sections.title: Leader
sections.text: Líder and dirigente overlap for a leader. Jefe emphasizes being in charge or holding authority; a leader need not be someone's boss.
examples: He is the leader of the group.

sections.title: Act
sections.text: Acto and acción overlap for an act. Hecho can name a deed but also a fact or event, whether or not someone deliberately did it.
examples: It was an act of generosity.

sections.title: Question
sections.text: Pregunta directly names a question asked. Cuestión may be a question under discussion, and asunto/tema mean a matter or topic rather than necessarily a question sentence.

sections.title: Matter
sections.text: Asunto, cuestión and tema overlap for a matter under discussion. Tema also means a theme or topic, and cuestión can be a question or problem.

sections.title: Photograph
sections.text: Foto is a shortened form of fotografía and remains feminine: una foto. Fotografía also names photography as an activity or art.

sections.title: Ground
sections.text: Suelo, tierra and terreno overlap in ground-related senses. Tierra can mean soil or land; terreno emphasizes a tract or type of land, and suelo also means a floor. Both tierra and suelo fit the selected soil cue: earth that supports plant growth.

sections.title: Floor
sections.text: Piso and suelo overlap for a floor surface. Piso also names a storey or an apartment in some regions; those meanings are separate.
examples: El suelo de la cocina está limpio.

sections.title: Room
sections.text: Habitación and cuarto overlap for a room. Sala commonly names a larger or public room or a living room; not every room is a sala.

sections.title: Food
sections.text: Comida and alimento overlap for food. Comida also means a meal, whereas alimento can be one foodstuff or nourishment.

sections.title: Meeting
sections.text: Reunión and encuentro can name a meeting. Sesión is a scheduled period of activity and need not be a meeting; encuentro can also be an accidental encounter.
examples: La reunión empieza a las diez.

sections.title: Memory
sections.text: Recuerdo is a specific memory. Memoria also names the faculty of remembering or stored information; those broader meanings do not all take recuerdo.
examples: Es un recuerdo de mi infancia.
It is a memory from my childhood.

sections.title: Freedom
sections.text: Libertad is freedom. Independencia means independence from control or dependence; a particular freedom is not necessarily complete independence.

sections.title: Increase
sections.text: Aumento and incremento overlap for an increase. Crecimiento is growth, which may be physical, numerical or developmental.
examples: There was an increase in prices.

sections.title: Evidence
sections.text: Prueba can be evidence, proof or a test. Evidencia can name evidence or obviousness; taking a test is not expressed by substituting evidencia for prueba.

sections.title: Advice
sections.text: Consejo and recomendación overlap for advice. Recomendación can also be an endorsement; consejo is countable in Spanish: un consejo.
examples: I will give you a piece of advice.

sections.title: Current
sections.text: Actual and presente overlap for current. Actual does not normally mean actual in the English sense of real; presente also means present rather than absent.

sections.title: True
sections.text: Cierto and verdadero overlap for true. Before a noun, cierto can mean a certain or some, which does not assert truth.

sections.title: Easy
sections.text: Fácil means easy. Sencillo can be easy or uncomplicated, but a simple task can still require great effort.

sections.title: Fundamental
sections.text: Básico and fundamental overlap for foundational importance. Básico can also mean elementary rather than advanced.

sections.title: Usual
sections.text: Habitual, normal and común overlap for what is usual. Normal can refer to a standard, and común can mean shared; neither always means frequent.

sections.title: Fast
sections.text: Rápido and veloz overlap for fast movement. Rápido also describes something taking little time.

sections.title: Full
sections.text: Lleno describes something filled. Completo means complete, with nothing missing; pleno can mean full or complete in particular combinations, but does not replace lleno for every container.

sections.title: Old
sections.text: Viejo and antiguo overlap for old objects. Antiguo can mean ancient or former; viejo also refers to old age and can sound blunt when applied to a person.

sections.title: Young
sections.text: Joven is young, or a young person as a noun. Adolescente identifies adolescence specifically; not every young person is an adolescent.

sections.title: Free
sections.text: Libre concerns freedom or availability. Gratis means without charge; something can be libre without being gratis, or gratis without being unrestricted.

sections.title: Perhaps
sections.text: Quizá and quizás are spelling variants with the same meaning. Acaso can also mean perhaps but has distinct uses in questions and por si acaso.

sections.title: Especially
sections.text: Especialmente and particularmente overlap for especially or particularly. The emphasis depends on the sentence, not a strict division between the two.

sections.title: Finally
sections.text: Finalmente can mean finally or lastly. Por fin emphasizes an awaited outcome and is two words; not every final item carries that sense of relief.

sections.title: Soon
sections.text: Pronto means soon. Temprano means early relative to a schedule or usual time; an early event need not be soon.

sections.title: Above
sections.text: Arriba describes an upper place or direction. Encima commonly uses de for above or on top of a named thing; sobre takes its complement directly.
examples: El libro está encima de la mesa.
The book is on top of the table.

sections.title: Behind
sections.text: Detrás de explicitly relates a position to something else. Atrás often means backward or at the back and can also describe past time; usage with complements varies regionally.

sections.title: Even
sections.text: Incluso, adverbial hasta and aun can mean even. Hasta also means until or as far as; aún with an accent means still or yet.

sections.title: To learn
sections.text: Aprender is learning or acquiring a skill. Estudiar is studying, which may lead to learning; enseñar is teaching someone else.

sections.title: To study
sections.text: Estudiar describes study; aprender describes learning or acquiring knowledge. The activity and its result are distinct.

sections.title: To hand over
sections.text: Entregar emphasizes delivery or handing over. Dar is broader but also fits giving an object to someone.

sections.title: To build
sections.text: Construir and edificar overlap for buildings. Construir also applies to arguments, machines and other things that are not buildings.

sections.title: To grow
sections.text: Crecer describes a child growing. Aumentar generally concerns an amount or magnitude; a child is not normally the subject of aumentar in this sense.

sections.title: To die
sections.text: Morir is die; matar is kill. Fallecer is a formal alternative for a person's death, and morirse is a common pronominal form.

sections.title: To kill
sections.text: Matar takes the being killed as its object. Morir describes dying, not causing another's death.

sections.title: To mention
sections.text: Mencionar and citar overlap when referring to someone or something. Citar can also quote a source or summon a person.

sections.title: To cite
sections.text: Citar can mention a source or quote it. Mencionar means mention; it does not by itself promise exact quotation.

sections.title: To support
sections.text: Apoyar and respaldar overlap for giving support. Sostener can support physically or maintain an argument; context determines the overlap.

sections.title: To hold up
sections.text: Sostener and sujetar can hold an object in place. Mantener is broader keeping in a state; it does not always describe physical support.

sections.title: To apply
sections.text: Aplicar puts a rule or method into practice. Usar is broader use; the words overlap in some contexts but have different constructions.

sections.title: To work
sections.text: Funcionar describes a machine or system working. Trabajar commonly describes work or labor; it is not a general replacement for funcionar.

sections.title: Worker
sections.text: Trabajador is anyone who works. Empleado is an employee; a self-employed worker need not be an empleado.

sections.title: Employee
sections.text: Empleado specifies an employment relationship. Trabajador is broader and also includes people working independently.

sections.title: Writer
sections.text: Escritor and autor overlap for a writer of literary works. Autor also names the creator of a nonwritten work or the perpetrator of an act.

sections.title: Author
sections.text: Autor and escritor overlap for a book's writer. Autor also applies to other creators; escritor specifically concerns writing.

sections.title: Eyesight
sections.text: Vista and visión overlap for eyesight. Vista also names a view; visión can name a vision or perspective.

sections.title: Vision
sections.text: Visión and vista overlap for visual ability. A vision of the future is another use of visión.

sections.title: Period
sections.text: Período and época overlap for time periods. Época often evokes an era characterized by events or conditions; duration is determined by context.

sections.title: Era; period
sections.text: Época and período overlap for a time period. Época often evokes a historically or personally characterized era.

sections.title: Source
sections.text: Fuente can be an information source, fountain or spring. Origen overlaps with source as origin, not a physical fountain.

sections.title: Post; position
sections.text: Cargo, puesto and posición overlap for an organizational role. Cargo also means a charge or responsibility; those uses need context.

sections.title: Term
sections.text: Término can be a word or an ending. Fin overlaps with the ending sense, not the lexical-item sense selected here.

sections.title: Object
sections.text: Objeto can be a thing or a purpose. Objetivo is an aim; it does not name every physical object.

sections.title: Being
sections.text: Ser and organismo overlap for a living entity. The noun ser is distinct from the infinitive ser, to be.

sections.title: Plant
sections.text: Planta can be a plant, a factory or a storey. Piso overlaps with storey, not the living-plant sense.

sections.title: Entrance
sections.text: Entrada and acceso overlap for an entrance. Entrada also means admission or a ticket in some contexts.

sections.title: Access
sections.text: Acceso concerns access or a way in. Entrada may name a physical entrance; access can be permission rather than a doorway.

sections.title: Club
sections.text: Club is a kind of association organized around an interest. Asociación is broader and can name other organizations.

sections.title: Scene
sections.text: Escena is a scene; escenario can be a stage or setting. A performance's scene and its physical stage are distinct.

sections.title: Stage
sections.text: Escenario is a stage or setting. Escena can name a dramatic scene rather than the physical platform.

sections.title: Late
sections.text: Adverbial tarde means late and contrasts with temprano, early. The noun tarde means afternoon.

sections.title: Which one
sections.text: Cuál commonly asks for selection or identification. Qué can ask for a definition or appear before a noun; regional usage and construction affect overlap.

sections.title: To add
sections.text: Sumar names arithmetic addition and also adding to an amount. Añadir is broader adding; this cue selects arithmetic.
